reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Cholesterolosis is a benign condition in which cholesterol esters and triglycerides accumulate within lipid-laden macrophages in the lamina propria of the gallbladder mucosa, producing yellow flecks against a hyperaemic mucosa (the strawberry gallbladder appearance)
It is subdivided into a diffuse (planar) form and a polypoid form, the latter giving rise to cholesterol polyps, the commonest type of gallbladder polyp
Most cases are asymptomatic incidental findings at ultrasound or on histology after cholecystectomy, and it is not premalignant

Cholesterol polyps are typically small, may be multiple, and characteristically show comet-tail or twinkling artefact and lack of vascularity or growth, features that help distinguish them from neoplastic polyps
Symptoms, when present, resemble biliary colic and are often related to coexisting gallstones, cholesterol crystals, or occasional detachment of a polyp causing transient obstruction

Polyp size and morphology guide management: small typical cholesterol polyps are followed by ultrasound surveillance, while larger, growing, sessile, or otherwise atypical polyps prompt consideration of cholecystectomy
It is part of the spectrum of hyperplastic cholecystoses along with adenomyomatosis, though the two are histologically and mechanistically distinct
The condition is unrelated to systemic hypercholesterolaemia and reflects local disturbance of gallbladder cholesterol handling rather than serum lipid levels
reference.pathophysiology: Cholesterolosis arises from a local abnormality of cholesterol metabolism within the gallbladder wall in which excess cholesterol, derived from cholesterol-supersaturated bile, is absorbed across the mucosa and esterified. The esterified cholesterol and triglyceride accumulate within macrophages (foam cells) that aggregate in the lamina propria at the tips of the mucosal villi, producing the yellow speckling of the diffuse form. Where these lipid-laden aggregates enlarge and become covered by hyperplastic epithelium on a slender stalk, they form pedunculated cholesterol polyps that project into the lumen. The deposits are confined to the mucosa without inflammation or muscular hypertrophy, distinguishing cholesterolosis from adenomyomatosis. Although the process shares the biliary cholesterol supersaturation that also underlies cholesterol gallstones, it correlates poorly with serum cholesterol concentrations, indicating that altered mucosal handling and biliary lipid composition, rather than systemic hyperlipidaemia, are the key drivers.
additionalDifferentials: Adenomatous or other neoplastic gallbladder polyp
Adherent gallstone or biliary sludge ball mimicking a polyp
Inflammatory polyp associated with chronic cholecystitis
Early gallbladder carcinoma presenting as a polypoid lesion
Gallbladder metastasis or, rarely, a mesenchymal tumour
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal ultrasound characterising polyp size, number, echotexture, and any comet-tail or twinkling artefact
Serial ultrasound surveillance to assess polyp stability or growth over time
Contrast-enhanced or high-resolution ultrasound to evaluate vascularity of indeterminate polyps
Endoscopic ultrasound for detailed assessment of larger or atypical polyps
MRI with MRCP when the biliary tree or an indeterminate lesion needs further characterisation
Histological examination of the cholecystectomy specimen for definitive diagnosis
redFlags: A gallbladder polyp that is large, sessile, or shows interval growth on surveillance
A solitary polyp associated with wall thickening or loss of normal wall layering
Coexisting gallstones with a polyp in an older patient or one with primary sclerosing cholangitis, raising malignancy risk
New or progressive jaundice or biliary obstruction
Detected vascularity within a polyp suggesting a neoplastic lesion
reference.prognosis: Cholesterolosis is entirely benign with an excellent prognosis, carries no malignant potential, and typically requires no treatment when asymptomatic; symptomatic patients or those with polyps meeting resection criteria are cured by cholecystectomy.
pitfalls: Assuming any gallbladder polyp is a benign cholesterol polyp and thereby missing a neoplastic lesion that meets resection or surveillance criteria
Attributing biliary symptoms to cholesterolosis when coexisting gallstones are the true cause
Confusing cholesterolosis with adenomyomatosis, which is a distinct hyperplastic cholecystosis
Wrongly linking the condition to serum hypercholesterolaemia and instituting unnecessary lipid investigation
Failing to arrange appropriate surveillance for polyps that fall below the threshold for immediate surgery
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Blumgart's Surgery of the Liver, Biliary Tract and Pancreas
management: Reassure and avoid intervention in asymptomatic incidental cholesterolosis, which is benign and not premalignant
Follow small typical cholesterol polyps with periodic ultrasound surveillance for stability and growth
Offer laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic disease or for polyps that are larger, growing, sessile or otherwise atypical
Perform cholecystectomy where symptomatic coexisting gallstones or biliary colic are present
Discharge from surveillance small polyps that remain stable over time
